articles.title: Rocket Mortgage founder Dan Gilbert turns his $1 billion Detroit redevelopment commitment into a nonprofit pledge; he will take no profits as the $2.2 billion project remakes Renaissance Center and 35-acre riverfront
articles.summary: Billionaire Rocket Mortgage founder Dan Gilbert is directing a massive $1 billion financial pledge toward the redevelopment of Detroit’s iconic
articles.body: Billionaire Rocket Mortgage founder Dan Gilbert is directing a massive $1 billion financial pledge toward the redevelopment of Detroit’s iconic Renaissance Center and the surrounding east riverfront through a newly formed nonprofit organisation. As per the official announcement, this philanthropic gift is believed to be the largest contribution to a non-profit redevelopment initiative in the history of American cities. Gilbert and his companies will receive no profits from the redevelopment of the Renaissance Center and 35-acre waterfront district. Gilbert's contribution will not be repaid.Under the structure, the nonprofit entity will hold full ownership of the real estate and channel any future financial surplus straight back into community initiatives. The move alters the ownership framework and beneficiaries of the broader $2.2 billion redevelopment plan, which is currently seeking roughly $548 million in public support.Zero profit, no repayment: How the structure operatesGilbert’s $1 billion commitment will not be repaid, and neither Gilbert nor any of his affiliated commercial companies will take profits from the project. As per the key operational details of the arrangement, the entity, registered as a 501(c)(4) social welfare organisation, will own, build out and manage the RenCen complex and its adjacent 35-acre riverfront district.Gilbert’s primary real estate firm, Bedrock, will handle comprehensive project management services entirely free of charge. Moreover, incoming revenue will be prioritised to settle day-to-day operating costs, service outstanding debt, fund reserve accounts, and cover ongoing property reinvestment. Any remaining financial surplus will be deployed directly for broader community benefits.The inaugural board will feature Rev. Wendell Anthony, president of the Detroit branch of the NAACP, alongside former Rocket Companies CEO Bill Emerson.Gilbert stated that the nonprofit will remain dedicated to the project’s overarching community mission “in perpetuity.”A Philanthropic Shift Rather Than New CapitalGilbert had previously earmarked roughly $1 billion for the riverfront initiative through Bedrock as a private commercial commitment. The newly revealed blueprint converts that planned private investment into a philanthropic gift, rather than injecting fresh, additional capital on top of the original target."Dan's contribution is purely a gift — not even tax-deductible — that he can't get a penny of it back," Bedrock CEO Jared Fleisher told Axios.Fleisher emphasized that while Gilbert’s contribution has become a charitable pledge, the proposed $548 million in public incentives remains essential to make the $2.2 billion development financially feasible.Long known as the global corporate headquarters of General Motors, the Renaissance Center has seen its occupancy dwindle substantially in recent years, with project developers describing the aging complex as increasingly obsolete.As part of the transformation blueprint, major physical overhauls will include demolishing two of the existing RenCen office towers, converting remaining sections of the high-rise towers into modern housing units and flexible office spaces, and replacing expansive surface parking lots with a walkable waterfront district featuring public parks, entertainment hubs and open civic spaces.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bengaluru leads post-SIR voter activity as form 6 applications rise 32%
articles.summary: Bengaluru tops Karnataka’s post-SIR voter updates: Form 6 inclusion requests up 32.4%, Form 7 deletion pleas up 291%, and Form 8 corrections up 19.2% (Sept 23–Oct 22).
articles.body: BENGALURU: Bengaluru recorded Karnataka’s highest number of applications for inclusion, deletion and correction of voter details after the special intensive revision (SIR) claims deadline, even as Form 6 applications rose 32.4% and deletion requests surged 291.48% across the state.Karnataka received 2.6 lakh Form 6 applications seeking inclusion in electoral rolls between Sept 23 and Oct 22.Form 7 applications seeking deletions or objecting to inclusions rose by 1.7 lakh, while 2.1 lakh Form 8 applications were filed for corrections and address changes, up 19.2% during the past one month.Bengaluru Urban topped Form 6 applications with 26,654, followed by Belagavi (17,437) and BBMP South (13,755), North (12,070) and Central (11,719) zones. Deletion requests were the highest in Bengaluru Urban (21,999), BBMP South (18,578) and BBMP North (17,471), followed by Dakshina Kannada (8,255) and Tumakuru (6,707).Bengaluru Urban also led Form 8 applications with 12,255, followed by Belagavi (11,680), Dakshina Kannada (11,487), Vijayanagara (9,051) and Mysuru (9,021), according to CEO office data.Bengaluru’s low re-entryBengaluru’s voter base of 1.03 crore before SIR saw a large number of electors marked absent, shifted, dead, duplicate or otherwise categorised (ASDDO) in the draft rolls. During the claims and objections period from Aug 24 to Sept 23, the region received only 2.2 lakh Form 6 applications for inclusion — around 5% of the ASDDO count.The CEO’s office has not disclosed how many applicants were new voters, leaving it unclear how many excluded electors sought re-entry. Karnataka’s draft rolls recorded 1.07 crore ASDDO deletions, most of them in Bengaluru. articles.title: Court acquits rape accused in UP, puts woman’s father in dock
articles.summary: Court in Ambedkar Nagar acquits kidnapping-rape accused Ramakant Verma as survivor and parents retract; orders complaint against father for false evidence.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: A special court in Ambedkar Nagar has acquitted a man accused of abducting and raping a woman, citing lack of evidence against him..Ramakant Verma alias Monu Verma was accused of abducting a young woman in Ambedkar Nagar and taking her to Mumbai where he raped her.Special Judge (SC/ST Act) Chintaram noted that the alleged survivor and her parents had retracted their earlier statements and did not support the allegations made in the complaint.The court also ordered the registration of separate proceedings against the complainant, Radheyshyam, for giving false evidence. It directed that the money provided by govt in connection with the case be deposited with the social welfare department within one month. The matter against the complainant has been scheduled for hearing on Nov 22.According to the prosecution, Radheyshyam had submitted a complaint at the Jahangirganj police station on July 17, 2019, stating that his daughter, 20, had left home to relieve herself on May 18, 2019, but did not return.After searching for her, the family lodged a missing-person report.He claimed that his daughter returned home crying on the evening of July 8 and told the family that Ramakant along with two unidentified men, had forcibly taken her to Mumbai. She was allegedly assaulted and abused there. The complaint further alleged that the accused threatened to kill her if she reported the matter when she was dropped near the Jahangirganj intersection.Police had registered an FIR under relevant provisions relating to kidnapping, assault, verbal abuse, criminal intimidation and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. After completing the investigation, police filed a chargesheet against the accused, including charges of rape and other offences. The court framed charges in Jan 2020.During the trial, the woman told the court that someone had grabbed her from behind while she was returning from a field late at night, but she could not identify the person.She further stated that the FIR had been lodged under pressure from villagers and that she had given statements to the police under pressure.Radheyshyam told the court that his daughter had gone to her maternal grandparents’ home after becoming upset over being scolded. articles.title: Gunmen kill at least 10 people in eastern Nigeria, police say
articles.summary: Nigerian police say a large group carried out the attack on Binnari village in Taraba State.
articles.body:
Gunmen have killed at least 10 people in an attack ⁠⁠on a village in eastern Nigeria, police said, as the country continues to battle banditry and armed groups in several parts of Nigeria.

Nigerian police said on Saturday that 10 bodies had been recovered as of Friday evening after a large group of gunmen on motorcycles attacked Binnari village in Taraba State.

According to police, the attackers also looted food from shops.

Survivors told the AFP news agency that at least 20 people were killed, while human rights group Amnesty International said in a statement on Saturday that the death toll was 40.

Amnesty International also said that while police ⁠had earlier confirmed the killing of 10 people, more bodies were recovered later on Saturday.

The gunmen opened fire just after Friday prayers, residents said.

“After the attackers left, we counted more than 20 bodies, and some people were still missing,” Binnari resident Sa’idu Nuhu told AFP.

Resident Isiyaku Musa also gave a death toll of at least 20.

Malam Abubakar Saifullahi, a community leader, told AFP that the attackers arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece, before raiding the village.

“They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions. They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack,” Saifullahi said.

Amnesty International criticised the Nigerian authorities, saying they “continue to leave rural communities in some parts of the north at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly committing atrocities with impunity”.

Banditry has become a growing issue in northwest and central Nigeria, with powerful gangs battling overstretched police and military across hard-to-reach, rural locations.

Taraba, a central-eastern state, also faces the non-ideological threat of “bandit” gangs.

Bandits raid villages, kidnap people for ransom, and levy “taxes” on farmers or miners in rural areas of Nigeria with little state presence.

Nigeria has also been fighting an armed rebellion since Boko Haram’s 2009 uprising.

Separately, on Saturday, the Nigerian military said it had killed 15 “terrorists” in northeastern Borno state in an air strike.

articles.title: Bukangi: Will the shark leave the Busan canal and make it back to sea?
articles.summary: More than a million people flocked to Busan to catch a glimpse of the female dusky shark they called Bukangi.
articles.body:
As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.

He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.

South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.

With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.

The first task was to determine the species.

Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.

The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.

A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.

They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.

Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.

As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.

Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".

People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.

Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.

City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.

A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.

Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.

Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.

More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.

The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.

"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for her… It's a lot of fun."

But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.

As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.

Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.

At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.

But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.

On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.

At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.

The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.

It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.

With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.

On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".

When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"

"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."

Others thought it was time for her to return home.

"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."

People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.

"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."

Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.

"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."

Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.

On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.

This left her trapped between the two layers.

Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.

Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.

There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.

Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.

She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.

But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.

For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.

articles.title: Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'
articles.summary: The meticulously-planned visit takes in three countries in nine days - but is not without jeopardy.
articles.body:
The planning is meticulous and dates back months, sometimes years, but there is always jeopardy.

King Charles III's visit to the Caribbean, which starts on Tuesday, takes him to three countries in nine days: the Bahamas, Guyana and finally Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).

It also throws him directly into the heat of the debate over the payment of reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade - alongside questions of whether the King should be apologising for the UK's role in what he has previously described as an "appalling atrocity" that leaves an "indelible stain" on history.

"This is the biggest risk of his reign so far with so much just outside of his control," said author and historian Sir Anthony Seldon. "Questions about slavery, reparations and apologies mean the moral integrity of the monarchy is being questioned."

The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.

A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.

The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.

Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.

But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.

This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.

Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.

Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.

Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

The leadership in the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda will celebrate the King and his work in protecting rainforests, creating cultural ties and reinforcing relationships around trade, energy, and agriculture.

But they do so against a backdrop of change.

The leaders of all three countries have voiced their support for reparatory justice.

In Antigua and Barbuda and the Bahamas, where the King is head of state, the conversation about becoming a republic has significant support.

Elected officials in the former no longer have to pledge allegiance to the King ending a 40-year tradition of swearing loyalty to the monarch.

"He pulled off an extraordinary triumph with President Trump in his US visit earlier this year and stood up to him and put him in his place in a way that no leader has done - while not incurring his wrath," said Sir Anthony. "If he can deal with the delicate nature of this trip for him personally, for the British monarchy, and the future of the Commonwealth, it could be an enormous success."

This Caribbean tour has to cut through a sea of royal distractions.

The King has spent much of the past three months in Scotland, where he is based over the summer.

It should have been a quieter time in the royal calendar, but it has been quite the opposite.

The surprise return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to the UK has been noisy. The level of coverage Harry and Meghan get is unsettling and, at times, irritating for the Royal Family.

The King's youngest son has not yet seen his father in person, but they are said to have talked.

Then enter Earl Spencer, the King's former brother-in-law, with his memoir, Swan Song, criticising the King's response to the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. It triggered a strong pushback from the Palace.

And in recent days, the serious claims made about Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, have drawn his daughter into a complex tale involving global police forces, sexual abuse allegations and further family trauma.

An impactful and successful Caribbean tour is a chance to switch focus.

But if royal stories back home are running hot, it can be hard to focus minds on the King's engagements over four thousand miles (6,437km) away.

Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy, who has strong family ties to the Caribbean, has accompanied the King on a number of trips outside the UK.

"He is our head of state. He is amongst some of the most recognisable figures in the world. For a small country like Guyana, the validation of a state visit is huge," said the Tottenham MP whose father came to the UK from what was then British Guiana and who also has relatives in Antigua and Barbuda. "My mother would forever recall the Queen's visit in 1996."

But there was also a recognition of that royal trip jeopardy.

"Knowing Guyana, Antigua and Barbuda as well as I do, he will be overwhelmingly received positively," Lammy said. "But these are lively democracies in which of course there will be some dissent."

A transatlantic flight, three countries over nine days and about 36 separate engagements when you're closing in on your 78th birthday is an intense schedule. It is also a reminder that the King is still dealing with a cancer diagnosis and having regular treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated its position that he is on a "positive trajectory".

Queen Camilla will only accompany the King on the Antigua and Barbuda leg of the visit for Chogm and a number of other engagements, including some around her own areas of interest – literacy and supporting efforts to end violence against women and girls.

The Queen, who will be 80 next July, is known to find the pace and hot conditions of some royal tours gruelling.

This is a trip that comes with potential pitfalls but also the possibility of great reward for the King.

"The King can be an extraordinarily empathetic and in tune figure," Sir Anthony said.

articles.title: The row over military service that could shape Israel's future
articles.summary: The ultra-Orthodox community is resisting being drafted into the Israeli army. But will they now bring down the Netanyahu government?
articles.body:
Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.

The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.

The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.

This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.

As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.

Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.

National security and the economy are two of the key issues this election. That means the division between the ultra-Orthodox and the majority of Israelis who believe they are not contributing their fair share to either is starker than ever.

With no outright majority likely for any current political alliance, and the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in doubt, the role of smaller parties - including Haredi parties - will once again be crucial in deciding who will govern Israel.

To have any chance of staying in power, Netanyahu needs to keep the ultra-Orthodox parties on side, however much pressure there is within Israel for their special status to be diminished.

From the ultra-Orthodox perspective, their social contract with the Israeli state is increasingly coming under pressure. Their all but exclusive focus on the study of Judaism's religious texts - such as the Torah, the Jewish Bible - means their education system is separate and many Haredim are not part of Israel's workforce.

For the ultra-Orthodox, the biggest issue of all is holding on to the exemption from serving in the IDF for students at traditional religious - or yeshiva - institutions. This dates back to the earliest days of the Israeli state when the Haredim were a miniscule community of survivors struggling to rebuild from the near extinction of the Holocaust.

But as Israel has become more embattled after the attacks of October 7, fighting wars on several fronts, their near complete absence from the country's conscription army has become more controversial.

Religious students and their rabbis believe that if young ultra-Orthodox men enter the military, they will be exposed to influences and behaviours that may decisively turn them away from their community. Beyond that, they believe that their staying true to the traditions of their community is vital for the very survival not only of Israel but the Jewish people.

When asked not long after October 7 why the ultra-Orthodox didn't contribute more to the military in such an emergency, one of the community's most senior leaders, Rabbi Dov Landau, said that not only should religious students not serve in the army, but they shouldn't even visit the wounded or attend the funerals of soldiers.

The rabbi said that in a time of such danger, only Torah students could protect Israel spiritually. "Salvation only comes through Torah learning, orderly Torah learning. And any neglect of or disruption to Torah learning, woe and alas for what will happen… The more Torah learners multiply, the more Torah learners increase their learning, the better. They protect us."

It would be a considerable understatement to say that this view is not shared by wider Israeli society. Polls have shown public support for conscripting the ultra-Orthodox surge throughout the war in Gaza. Many see it as a dereliction of responsibility by the Haredi community, made all the more galling by the fact that such a stance comes at the expense of taxpayers. The IDF has bemoaned a deficit in manpower, while many Israelis have had to serve hundreds of days in the past three years.

Dahlia Scheindlin is a leading political consultant and pollster in Israel. She says this issue is critical for Netanyahu and is key to understanding this moment in Israeli society against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, particularly among the political right. "Really the most burning, more immediate issue is the right-wing communities who are furious at the government for protecting the blanket exemption from the IDF at a time when, especially among the right, but really everybody in the Jewish community in Israel, is serving and many dying in these wars."

Two years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from serving in the military was effectively null and void. That could have meant that those dedicated to full-time religious study would now be drafted.

The reaction from the Haredi community was one of fury. Hundreds of thousands of Haredim held protests, blocking the main highways. And as with the incident in Modi'in, they tried to prevent the arrest of religious students for evading conscription. Protests have continued off and on, and densely-populated Haredi areas are often the backdrops for confrontation with the security forces.

This is a row that is playing out in the election.

There are two parties that have traditionally represented the Haredi community. One is United Torah Judaism – or UTJ – and represents Ashkenazi Jews, or Jews of European origin. The other is Shas, which was formed later and represents the Sephardi and Mizrahi – Jews from North Africa and the Middle East. They share a core agenda, which puts religious study above all else, including any questions around relations with the Palestinians.

Both UTJ and Shas have been part of Netanyahu's coalition - and they used their political clout to find ways to try to block enforcement of the Supreme Court ruling. On several occasions, they threatened to pull out of the alliance and bring the government down. UTJ acted on this but continued to support the government from outside, while Shas remained within the coalition.

Centre-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, who's shaped up as Netanyahu's main rival in this month's election, does not support their stance. He has made clear his belief that the idea of the ultra-Orthodox constituting a separate state within Israel with its own rules has become increasingly toxic. "A country that sends its best sons and daughters to fight and sacrifice their lives cannot tolerate a reality in which a state within a state exists," he said.

All this has meant that the issue of conscription exemption for ultra-Orthodox men is the number one priority on the electoral agenda of both Shas and UTJ.

A recent remark by a UTJ parliamentary candidate, Eliakim Stark, has raised the temperature further. He compared the plight of ultra-Orthodox men evading the military draft to the persecution of Jews during the Holocaust. It triggered furious rebukes from opposition leaders from across the political spectrum.

Daniel Goldman, an activist who specialises in Haredi issues, says that the two main Haredi parties feel increasingly embattled and less open to compromise.

He says the ultra-Orthodox don't believe that the state really needs their boys to bolster numbers. "It's at least partly down to the fact that the Haredi parties see the state as wanting to take their boys out of the community and change them from ultra-Orthodox to either regular religious or secular, God forbid, as they perceive it," he says. "And so in that environment of tension, they've actually hardened their positions."

Yitzhak Goldknopf from the UTJ, a former minister, has gone so far as to issue an ultimatum: "The Haredim will not change their way of life because there is an army and a war... If there is no choice and they must leave the country, they will leave."

But this is having a clear impact on the electoral fortunes of the Netanyahu coalition - of which Shas in particular has long been a key part. Without them, Netanyahu's alliance would fall short of the more than 60 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.

Dahlia Scheindlin, the Israeli pollster, says that the refusal to give up the draft exemption by Shas and UTJ is damaging Netanyahu's coalition. "It is one of the main reasons why the coalition is unable to win back the kind of support that they had in 2022 when they won 64 seats," she says. "They're currently polling at about 50 to 52 seats."

All Netanyahu's challengers advocate for ending the ultra-Orthodox exemption and cutting funds to institutions or individuals who refuse the draft. On the left, Yair Golan has called for an immediate mobilisation of those who are eligible.

So, despite statements from Shas and UTJ that they would switch allegiance from Netanyahu if he were to dilute his support, there seems for now nowhere else for them to go.

Anshel Pfeffer has been a leading commentator on the Israeli political scene for years - now mainly as the Economist's correspondent in Israel. He says Netanyahu's position looks shaky. "There are two things that are bringing together the current opposition bloc," he says. "One is obviously they want to replace Netanyahu and the other is they are capitalising on this really hostile environment nowadays towards the ultra-Orthodox, mainly over the issue of the draft to the army.

"Netanyahu has been willing for many years, to basically give the ultra-Orthodox whatever they want. They're not going to get that from the opposition."

Into this arena of resentment and intransigence, a new Haredi party has emerged this year, presenting itself as a break with the traditional mindset of Shas and UTJ.

Essentially, the Haredi Public Party is offering a compromise in which the ultra-Orthodox would contribute more to Israel as a whole while maintaining the core of their identity.

For the first time in the ultra-Orthodox community, it is also fielding two female candidates.

One of them, Ziva Ginz, explained to the BBC her party's position on the military draft. Key to it is men serving being allowed to remain culturally Haredi. "Anyone whose life is genuinely devoted to full-time Torah study should be able to continue learning. Everyone who isn't sitting and studying for a full day should serve alongside the rest of Israeli youth, in frameworks where a young man can enter as a Haredi and finish as a Haredi," she says.

But it may be too soon for such efforts at compromise to make an impact this election.

Anshel Pfeffer says that it's difficult to sway the base vote in the ultra-Orthodox community, where most still essentially follow what their rabbi says they should do.

"And once people are voting for other parties, they won't necessarily do so for another Haredi party," Pfeffer explains. "That's why we're seeing people like [far-right leader and National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir making inroads in the Haredi community, because he's the only non-Haredi party leader who actually talks to young Haredi. Basically, every other party in Israel doesn't even try."

This is reflected in the polls, which show his Jewish Power party is making gains.

If Ben Gvir's actions are increasingly seen as tainting Israel's international image with his support for policies such as annexing the occupied West Bank, his hard-right message is attracting a bigger core of support within the country. His ultra-nationalist ethos is not one that traditionally overlaps with policies of the Haredi parties, but they share a position on the right of Israeli politics.

So for some ultra-Orthodox voters looking for a new political home, Ben Gvir represents the nearest alternative. His self-portrayal as a strong man unafraid to take an extreme position against those he perceives as Israel's enemies in the face of international condemnation may attract some already leaning to the far right in the Haredi community.

No alliance appears close to achieving a majority, however, so there is bound to be a lot of horse trading to secure a workable coalition after the vote.

Netanyahu will naturally apply his exceptional political skills to trying to find one way or another to stay in power.

As ever, that leaves the smaller parties with the ability to play the role of kingmaker. That's a role that the ultra-Orthodox parties have been known for in the past. But this time they may not be the decisive factor.

"The truth is, any small party can become a kingmaker," Dahlia Scheindlin says. "I don't think it would take too much to lure the Haredi parties away from Netanyahu... The thing is, though, I don't think the opposition parties will want to lure them in unless they have some promise that they're really prepared to make serious concessions on the draft. The opposition parties are absolutely staking their platforms and their promise to the voters on that issue."

This time, rather than being the kingmakers, it may turn out that the ultra-Orthodox parties help bring down the king.

articles.title: The PHP developer who became the unsung hero of the internet
articles.body:
For more than 20 years, Ondřej Surý has been quietly helping to keep websites around the world running securely, largely in his spare time.

He voluntarily maintains software for two of the most popular versions of Linux, a free operating system similar to Windows, which are often used on web servers.

Typically, this involves keeping them up-to-date with the latest version of PHP, a programming language which underpins a significant number of the world's websites.

With the help of AI, two major cyber-security flaws were identified in the programming language, leading the PHP Foundation to release fixes.

But average folk may struggle to understand how to install these onto their systems - so Surý, for free, dropped everything to convert the fixes into packages, which can be easily installed without expertise.

"The feeling is like I am responsible for all these people and I can't fail them," he told BBC News.

What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?

The vulnerabilities in PHP sparked an international scramble to install security updates, amid fears that cyber criminals could exploit the gaps.

Surý is one of a small number of developers whose work helps make those updates available.

And while keeping the internet secure might sound like a full-time occupation, it isn't actually his day job.

He works as director of DNS engineering at Internet Systems Consortium, a US non-profit organisation.

But in his spare time, he has spent more than two decades voluntarily maintaining PHP software packages for the Linux versions Debian and Ubuntu.

He takes the source code released by the PHP project and turns it into packages which website operators can easily install on their servers.

When asked how it felt to be described as one of the people who helped "save the internet" this week as some online put it, his response was modest.

"It's kind of fulfilling because I sense my work has a purpose," he said.

"At the same time, I feel that not enough credit has been given to other people who has been part of this, like the PHP project people."

But he also acknowledged the weight that comes with his role.

Surý had been given advanced warning about the vulnerabilities by the PHP project, but when information about the weaknesses leaked online, the planned release was brought forward and things started ramping up.

"I got aware that this is quite severe and I don't have that much time to prepare the packaging of the PHP that I provide to people," he said.

Despite the urgency, he said he was confident that his experience and preparation would allow him to get the job done.

Other developers around the world were also working to ensure the patches could be distributed - highlighting just how much of the internet's essential infrastructure sometimes depends on dedicated developers.

Surý said this week had prompted an outpouring of support from people who relied on his software packages.

He revealed that he received more than $10,000 (£7,470) in donations in just a few days.

"This week is basically about a year's worth of the contributions that I got before," he said.

He said major technology companies should take more responsibility for supporting the open source software they depend upon.

"I think they should be more responsible," he said.

"If you just take and don't give back then it will backfire."

Surý has also been considering what would happen if he could no longer maintain the software packages himself.

He said colleagues at software company Freexian could take over, but they do not yet have the same accumulated experience.

"Yes, that's pretty much true," he said, when I asked him whether much of the responsibility ultimately rested with him.

But he is concerned that AI may be dramatically accelerating the discovery of security vulnerabilities, helping both cyber criminals and those trying to stop them.

"I think this is was the most severe incident in years, but I think that because of the AI capabilities are getting better in the cyber security, this might not be an isolated incident," he said.

"And people should be prepared to act this quickly more often because incidents like this might happen in the future - in the near future."

articles.title: Kushner’s attorneys send notice to Vanity Fair on alleged “defamatory” excerpt
articles.summary: Attorneys representing President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner have sent a letter to Vanity Fair and Condé Nast over allegations published in an article on Thursday calling them “false” and “defamatory.” “We formally put Vanity Fair and Condé Nast on notice regarding the false and defamatory allegations published about our client, Jared Kushner,” wrote Chad Mizelle,…
articles.body:
Attorneys representing President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner have sent a letter to Vanity Fair and Condé Nast over allegations published in an article on Thursday calling them “false” and “defamatory.”

“We formally put Vanity Fair and Condé Nast on notice regarding the false and defamatory allegations published about our client, Jared Kushner,” wrote Chad Mizelle, former chief of staff of the U.S. Department of Justice, in a post on social platform X . “Serious questions are now being raised about the credibility of this reporting, including by independent journalists.”

Vanity Fair published an excerpt from a book by investigative journalist Matthew Cole titled “Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East .” The excerpt alleged Kushner’s hacked phone revealed his secret negotiations which include millions of dollars in transfers.

“Despite repeated requests, the author has failed to produce a single bank statement, wire transfer record, account number, or other verifiable evidence supporting these extraordinary accusations,” Mizelle said in his post with a copy of the letter attached.

“We have seen no indication that Vanity Fair conducted any independent verification of these claims before publishing them,” he added.

The letter signed says the accusations listed from the excerpt are “as false as” they are “outrageous” and since these allegations “charge our client with committing serious crimes, they are defamatory per se.”

The Hill has reached out to Clare for a copy of the letter and a comment.

The letter called for Vanity Fair to immediately remove the excerpt from its website and every other platform. It also asks the outlet to preserve records related to the publishing of the excerpt.

Earlier this month, CNN published a report alleging Kushner’s private equity firm had ties to a company heavily involved in Israel’s military. Kushner denied those allegations calling it a “a deeply misleading story.”

Kushner has served as a U.S. special envoy throughout Trump’s second term, playing an important role in leading peace talks between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Hamas, as well as with Ukraine and Russia .

articles.title: France sees another weekend of mass protests, with nearly 1,000 detained
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people protested across France Saturday, according to the country’s Interior Ministry, in what were largely peaceful demonstrations.
articles.body: Hundreds of thousands of people protested across France Saturday, according to the country’s Interior Ministry, in what were largely peaceful demonstrations. Around 110,000 of the over 410,000 protesters were in Paris, the ministry said, roughly the same number who demonstrated in the capital last weekend. Some protesters have been calling for greater investment in the country’s education system, more opportunities for its young workers and solutions to surging living costs. Nearly 1,000 people were detained amid demonstrations across France Saturday, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. This compares with 385 detentions amid the protests last week, he said. “In Paris, we had a major demonstration that took place peacefully, like most protest marches across the entire country,” Nuñez told reporters. Nuñez said the police had restricted protesters’ movements: “They were prevented from staging unauthorized roving protests or heading toward city centers.” “In certain cities there was some damage or looting of businesses, in very limited numbers,” Nuñez added, but far less than during protests a week ago. Nuñez said there had been “no targeted attacks” on public buildings such as town halls and police stations, as seen last weekend. However, security forces faced an “extremely high level of violence” Nuñez added, “with projectiles constantly being thrown and mortar fireworks fired.” He said security forces would remain deployed until very late Saturday evening local time to guard against looting. Some 70,000 police officers had been mobilized across the country Saturday, the Interior Ministry said, as French authorities launched an enormous security operation for the second round of protests. Specialist SWAT units, helicopters, armored vehicles, police dogs and water cannons were at the ready as part of the operation, after more than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. After a peaceful march through Paris, a crowd of several thousand protesters confronted police, who used tear gas and a water cannon to block them, according to a CNN team at the scene. The clashes broke out at the Porte de Vincennes, the endpoint of the march, which drew an estimated 110,000 people. In France’s second city, Marseille, protesters launched mortar fireworks toward police during running street skirmishes, and there were reports of looting in various parts of the city, including a jewelry store with smashed windows and a supermarket being pillaged, CNN’s French affiliate BFMTV reported. Images from Bordeaux, on France’s Atlantic coast, showed tear gas being used against protesters in the famous Place de la Bourse. Videos showed some masked protesters hurling objects at police as the tear gas drifted across the square. In Nice, dozens of far-right activists attacked people protesting peacefully Saturday, BFMTV reported. The leader of far-left party La France Insoumise, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, warned that nationwide industrial action will take place on November 5 if French President Emmanuel Macron does not respond to protesters’ demands. “A general strike, called by the CGT, looms over the government for the 5th of November,” he told BFMTV, while speaking from the front line of Saturday’s demonstration in Paris. As scores of protesters took to the streets in cities across France on Saturday, anti-government demonstrations were also taking place in a number of other European countries. In the Italian cities of Naples, Rome and Milan, stores boarded up their windows ahead of planned protests after looting in earlier demonstrations. Protesters in the Albanian capital Tirana set fires to dumpsters and threw stones and tear gas canisters. And in Brussels, students held up placards and barricaded streets. Police deployed a water cannon, according to Belgium’s public broadcaster VRT.

articles.title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
articles.summary: The PM said he wants a "factual" and "evidence-based debate" about returning to free movement between Britain and Europe.
articles.body:
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.

Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now.

"It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times.

"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."

He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it".

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said.

"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.

In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.

However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.

The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.

The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".

Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."

Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch".

"He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.

articles.title: Obama slams Trump’s ‘cruelty and corruption’ as he rallies Democrats
articles.summary: Former US president says Trump ‘chose to make a series of bad decisions’, highlighting the US-Israel war on Iran.
articles.body:
Barack Obama has criticised the “cruelty and corruption” during US President Donald Trump’s second term, as the former president campaigned for Democratic candidates in two Midwestern states.

Obama delivered scathing criticism of Trump on Saturday at a midterm election campaign rally in Ohio, slamming his successor’s foreign policies.

“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” the 65-year-old Democrat said in Cleveland. “Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” he added, referring to the US-Israel war on Iran.

Obama urged Ohioans to vote against the Republican administration, saying: “After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough’.”

Later on Saturday evening, Obama headed to Michigan to campaign for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson.

At the Detroit rally, he framed the November 3 vote as a “circuit breaker” to “at least rein in some of the foolishness” of Trump’s presidency. “We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting, ⁠on your dime, like this,” Obama said.

“Never seen a president so intent ⁠on selling favours like this,” he also said, adding that the Republican Party “seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government”.

Obama ridiculed the Trump ⁠administration’s claims of victory against Iran. He argued that the war has given Iran more economic leverage because its threats to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have unsettled oil exporters.

“Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, ‌where oil goes through to get to the world,” Obama said.

The former president also addressed the recent controversy in Ohio’s gubernatorial race surrounding an attack advertisement by Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy against Democrat Amy Acton.

“In recent days, we’ve seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to,” Obama said of Ramaswamy. “I don’t know what’s happened where the standards of behaviour are so low that somebody could run an ad like that.”

In the advertisement, Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, disputes her daughter’s account of a childhood involving homelessness and ⁠⁠⁠⁠sexual abuse by her stepfather, urging Ohioans not to vote for her.

Acton says she has not seen her mother since 1978. Acton’s brother has supported her account of being sexually abused by her stepfather when she was a child. The stepfather, who died in 2004, was charged with rape.

Obama backed Acton, saying that she has “spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she’s experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness”.

The former president shared the rally stage with Acton and Ohio’s former Democratic senator, Sherrod Brown.

Trump defended the Ramaswamy advertisement on Saturday, when he cast his ballot early in Florida.

Obama also condemned critics of El-Sayed, suggesting they are using the 41-year-old politician’s name and Muslim faith to tear him down.

“We have seen this movie before. I starred in it,” Obama told a rally in Detroit. “I’ve got a long-form birth certificate to prove it.”

He added, “Abdul is as Michigan as it gets.”

The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a “radical”, declaring that “Abdul shares my values”.

Obama remains the Democratic Party’s best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. And he is taking his star power on the road in the final days of the midterm elections, which will help determine the balance of power in US politics on November 3.

Obama will headline a Democratic Party rally in Georgia next week with Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms.

articles.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink’s slowdown in Ukraine
articles.summary: Elon Musk on Saturday alluded to being behind last week’s Starlink slowdown in Ukraine which impacted the country’s military capabilities. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a post on social platform X. The slowdown happened…
articles.body:
Elon Musk on Saturday alluded to being behind last week’s Starlink slowdown in Ukraine which impacted the country’s military capabilities.

“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a post on social platform X.

The slowdown happened as Ukraine’s military faced restricted access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink. It targeted Starlink-supported Ukrainian military drones, airplanes and helicopters traveling faster than 100 mph, a source familiar with the matter previously told The Hill. Musk initially claimed that the decisions to restrict the speed or usage of Starshield are made by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president.

He maintained his claim in Saturday’s post saying Starshield “is controlled by the US government. What they decide to do is up to them.”

“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk said in his post.

Earlier this week, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk ordered the slowdown of Starshield, following which several Democrats called for an investigation into the matter.

“Either the President was lying or Musk was lying, but the decision to slow down satellite speed and access has life or death consequences for Ukraine,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) wrote on social media . “This deserves a full investigation by the Senate. Elon Musk should be compelled to testify before Congress and under oath.”

On Friday, Ukraine’s military continued to struggle with a slowed Starlink satellite system. The Journal reported that Starshield connections continued to fail in most of the country if drones flew faster than 100 mph.

In his Saturday post, Musk said Starlink is “critical to the defense of Ukraine, as it is the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now. Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately.”

“This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact,” the SpaceX CEO continued.

articles.title: A 67,000-hectare cattle property in Australia faced a land-clearing case for years; a signed settlement will now protect 80 hectares along the Daly River
articles.summary: A 67,000-hectare cattle property in Australia's Northern Territory has reached a formally signed settlement following a prolonged legal dispute over
articles.body: A 67,000-hectare cattle property in Australia's Northern Territory has reached a formally signed settlement following a prolonged legal dispute over alleged unauthorised land clearing. The government first announced an agreement in March 2025, but it remained unsigned for more than a year as legal proceedings continued. The case concerned allegations that 286 hectares had been cleared without a permit. Under the settlement, the owners must revegetate and protect an approximately 80-hectare area along the Daly River. The agreement also provides for a registered covenant restricting future clearing and requiring the land to be protected for the benefit of the river environment.Why did the Claravale land-clearing case drag onAccording to ABC News, the legal dispute dates back to late 2023, when the then-Labor government initiated proceedings against Claravale following allegations of unpermitted land clearing. The action came amid national scrutiny of land clearing associated with the Northern Territory's cotton industry. The prosecution involved allegations that 286 hectares of the property had been cleared without the necessary permit, in contravention of the Territory's planning laws.According to the Northern Territory Department of Lands, Planning and Environment's Notice of Outcome – Claravale Farm prosecution matter, it received a complaint on 18 November 2021 alleging unpermitted clearing of native vegetation at NT Portion 1188, Dorisvale Road, Claravale, known as Claravale Farm. The department investigated the complaint, and on 14 November 2023, the Minister for Infrastructure, Planning and Logistics determined that the matter should be prosecuted. Charges were filed on 15 November 2023 against two individuals and a company for alleged breaches of section 75C(2) of the Planning Act 1999.How will the Claravale settlement protect the Daly RiverThe settlement establishes environmental protection measures along the Daly River, including the revegetation of an approximately 80-hectare area within Claravale Farm. According to the Department of Lands, Planning and Environment's notice, the agreement provides for a covenant in gross to be registered over the property. This covenant is intended to bind current and future landowners to restrictions on clearing and disturbing native vegetation within the designated area.Under the department's published terms, the protected area must be revegetated, kept free of weeds and not used for agricultural activities, industrial operations or other business endeavours. The covenant will protect native vegetation along the river's northern bank across a 1.5-kilometre section of Claravale Farm, with the protected strip extending 250 metres from the river. The covenant had been designed by the parties to improve environmental outcomes for the Daly River and bring Claravale Farm into line with the Northern Territory Planning Scheme Land Clearing Guidelines concerning native vegetation buffers along rivers.Why was the Claravale settlement delayedThe case continued after the government announced in March 2025 that a settlement had been reached. The agreement had not been signed by the owners, meaning the matter continued to be listed in court. The property owners and the neighbouring Claravale Farm were listed for sale in late 2025, with the owners seeking more than $30 million for the property. Earlier in 2026, the case was listed in the Darwin Local Court after the Northern Territory government attempted to prevent the property from being sold.The eventual settlement retained the original terms. In comments to the broadcaster, Burgoyne said he was pleased the matter had been finalised and that the land adjoining the Daly River would be protected into the future. The defendants acknowledged clearing vegetation without a permit on another section of Claravale Farm. The agreed settlement therefore combines the resolution of the prosecution with a legally registered mechanism intended to protect and restore a designated section of riverbank vegetation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Still more rain, evacuations remain in place from Four Corners region flooding
articles.summary: Hundreds of homes remained evacuated and without electricity Saturday after days of heavy rain — over 5 inches in places — surged water from the Colorado mountains into the New Mexico and Arizona desert.
articles.body: FORT COLLINS, Colo. — Hundreds of homes remained evacuated and without electricity Saturday after days of heavy rain — over 5 inches in places — surged water from the Colorado mountains into the New Mexico and Arizona desert. Even as the San Juan River and other streams receded from record highs, more storms rumbled through, causing local officials to warn of still more surges. “This is not over, and we need you to monitor alerts,” police Chief Steve Hebbe of Farmington, New Mexico, said in a news conference. The flooding affected some 2,000 people in and around the city of 46,000 not far from Four Corners, the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. At least a couple hundred people needed rescue — too many for busy officials to keep accurate count — since rains picked up Wednesday and flooding culminated Thursday and Friday. Some were stranded on rooftops. Rescues included 11 hoist operations involving New Mexico National Guard helicopters, each of which hauled as many as eight people to safety, San Juan County spokesperson Devin Neeley said. But shelters were not full, leading officials to suspect that most evacuees were staying with friends and family. Even with water levels having lowered, evacuations remained in effect until officials deem it safe to return. Potential hazards included downed power lines, leaking gas lines and the likelihood of yet more storms through the weekend. “There’s a lot of anxiety, and there’s a lot of frustration,” San Juan County Sheriff Shane Ferrari said. “But please understand we are blocking those areas for your safety.” Officials in Colorado and New Mexico urged people not to fly drones to check on their property or to sightsee, warning that such activity can endanger rescue aircraft. They also asked people not to use 911 except for true emergencies. Downstream from Farmington, the San Juan River flooded parts of the vast Navajo Nation. A 2-mile stretch of U.S. Highway 64 west of Shiprock was closed with water on the roadway. Upstream in Colorado, the milkshake-brown San Juan River raged through the hot springs resort town of Pagosa Springs at a level unseen in over a century. The flood was well over 2 feet higher than one just over a year ago that officials considered a 100-year flood. The Animas River raged in a muddy torrent through Durango, a southwest Colorado tourist city, though below records dating back over a century. Flooding extended as far east as the Conejos River in south-central Colorado, and Gov. Jared Polis added Conejos County to a list of places eligible for disaster help. Some routes including U.S. 160 northeast of Pagosa Springs remained closed. But the famous, winding Million Dollar Highway — formally U.S. 550 — reopened between Durango and Ouray after crews addressed an area of water damage. The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck the Grand Canyon and areas of New Mexico. The region’s rocky deserts are naturally prone to flash floods, but the rain has saturated soils, making flooding even likelier.

articles.title: Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents
articles.summary: The Renters' Rights Act gives greater flexibility to leave a tenancy but the changes have posed challenges for student landlords.
articles.body:
When the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.

The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.

Eddie Lever had finished his first year at the University of Exeter when he decided the course wasn't for him.

The 20-year-old wanted to switch to studying international relations at the University of York but had already organised his house for the upcoming year.

But because of changes in the Renters' Rights Act, Eddie only had to give two months' notice before he could leave and stop paying rent.

The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months. For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.

Instead, properties are now rented on a rolling basis, which means tenants pay rent weekly or monthly with no fixed end date.

University-owned halls of residence and Purpose-Built Student Accommodation are exempt and can still offer fixed-term contracts so this change primarily affects students renting from a private landlord.

"If the Renters' Rights Act wasn't a thing, I don't think I would have been able to move universities because I would have been locked into the full [year] contract," Eddie explains.

What the Renters' Rights Act means for tenants and landlords

'I fought for change to remove student housing stress'

More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs

As he was signed up to a joint tenancy, when he left it ended the tenancy for the whole house.

Fortunately, Eddie had a friend who was looking for a room who was able to take his place so his housemates could sign a new tenancy.

He acknowledges the situation would have been more difficult for his housemates if there wasn't someone who could take his room.

However, Eddie thinks the benefits for students are worth this risk.

"If you were to fall out with your flatmates or if you decide that university is not for you, being locked into a full-term contract can be really prohibitive financially," he says.

"So without that flexibility, people can really be locked into situations that they don't necessarily want to be in."

Lewis Wilson, vice president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says this flexibility means students can also save money on rent by moving home for the summer.

While previously, many student rental contracts ran into the summer after courses had finished, students can now choose to move out earlier if they want.

Wilson says students also benefit from wider changes in the act, which bans landlords in England from evicting tenants without a reason.

Campaigners argue this gives renters greater security and confidence to ask for repairs, without fearing they could be evicted if they raise concerns.

However, greater flexibility for students to leave tenancies also means less certainty for landlords.

The act did introduce a specific ground for landlords to evict a group of students at the end of the academic year if they intend to re-let the property to students.

Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association, says the bigger problem for student landlords is if their tenants choose to move out earlier.

He argues this is a bigger risk for students - who may fall out with their housemates or drop out of university - than, for example, families, who are less likely to want to move out after just a few months.

Norris says the end of fixed-term tenancies means student houses could be left empty over the summer after courses finish - or even earlier.

He adds that it is now more difficult for student landlords to rent a house for just a few months as they don't know how long the tenants will stay and can't guarantee it will be available for students again in the autumn.

Norris says it's early days for the new legislation and many landlords are taking this year as a test to see how these issues play out in practice.

However, he warns that some may choose to increase the monthly rent they charge to cover the risk of their properties being empty over the summer.

In some cases, he says landlords may even sell up or stop renting to students, reducing supply and pushing up prices.

Sue Lawes, who rents three shared houses to students in Norwich, is worried about the changes.

While Sue says she doesn't want to put up her prices, if her houses end up being empty over the summer because students decide to end their tenancy after their final exams she says she may have to.

She has already brought forward the start of her tenancy agreements to August instead of September to try and reduce the risks of this.

However, she says if her tenants move out earlier in the year she would struggle to make a profit, whilst covering costs including her mortgage, council tax and utility standing charges when the properties are empty.

She argues higher monthly rents would mean bigger upfront costs for students and higher overall costs for those who do choose to carry on renting over the summer.

Sue stresses that she supports the aim of the legislation to give tenants greater security and that students should be able to move out if their landlord is not carrying out repairs.

But she wants landlords to be allowed to offer fixed-term contracts to students in line with the academic year to avoid properties being left empty over the summer.

"Landlords are going to find it very, very hard to absorb those void periods," she says.

"Landlords will put prices up and students are going to pay."

articles.title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
articles.summary: Sources close to the duchess said she warned her father last year that he would never meet his grandchildren.
articles.body:
The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.

Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.

It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.

It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.

The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.

It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday , include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.

She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.

Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father

The force said it shared the letter with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time, although it did not pass on the contents to other law enforcement agencies.

The Met said it is now reviewing its handling of the matter.

In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan revealed the existence of the letter – saying it contained "disturbing allegations" about her father.

"I am deeply distressed," Meghan wrote. "My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Meghan is the only daughter of Thomas Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.

Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.

The Sun reported Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.

The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.
